uncited: The method integrates frequency-domain resampling into the Shear-Warp factorization pipeline.
It transforms the volume to the frequency domain, applies shifts and zooms via zero-padding and phase multiplication, and transforms back to the spatial domain for compositing and warping.
*   **Volume Data:** Real-valued array $V$.
*   **Frequency Domain Data:** Complex-valued array $\hat{V}$.
*   **Intermediate Image:** 2D array storing color and transparency (density) values.
*   **Sampling distance in k-direction ($s$):** Controls the resolution along the view axis.
*   **Zoom factor:** Applied in $i$ and $j$ directions.
Compute the 3D Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) of the volume $V$ to obtain $\hat{V}(u,v,w)$.
*   Apply the derivative theorem: multiply by $i \cdot 2\pi u$, $i \cdot 2\pi v$, and $i \cdot 2\pi w$ respectively in the frequency domain to compute partial derivatives.

*   Compute the Inverse 3D DFT to get gradient components $
abla V_x, 
abla V_y, 
abla V_z$.
Calculate shear coefficients $(s_i, s_j)$ and translation values $(t_i, t_j)$ based on the viewing direction [Lac95].
The displacement of the $k$-th slice in $i$ and $j$ directions is denoted $a_{ik}$ and $a_{jk}$.
*   Calculate the desired sampling distance $s'$ in the $k$-direction.
*   Round $K'$ to the closest integer $K_{0 \text{ pad}}$.
*   Zero-pad $\hat{V}$ in the $w$-direction (frequency domain corresponding to $k$) to size $K_{0 \text{ pad}}$.
*   Perform an Inverse Fourier Transform (IFFT) in the $k$-direction only.
The $i$ and $j$ directions remain in the frequency domain.
*   Determine desired slice resolution $(I_0, J_0)$.
*   Calculate required padding $I_{0 \text{ pad}}$ and $J_{0 \text{ pad}}$ to achieve the new period.
*   Zero-pad the data in the $u$ and $v$ directions (frequency domain corresponding to $i$ and $j$).
*   **Frequency Domain Shift:** Apply the shifting theorem to $\hat{V}$ by multiplying by phase shifts $e^{-i 2\pi a_{xkFD} \cdot \text{freq}}$ to achieve the fractional shift.
*   **Spatial Domain Shift:** Perform an Inverse Fourier Transform in the $i$ and $j$ directions.
Apply the integer shift $a_{xkSD}$ by moving the slice data in the spatial domain.
*   Apply transfer functions to the resampled slices.
*   Composite slices along the $k$-axis into a 2D intermediate image using the "over" operator [PD84].
*   Apply a 2D warping transformation to the intermediate image to produce the final image.
*   Transform pixel coordinates from image space to sheared-object space using the inverse warping matrix.
*   **Zoom Precision:** Zooming is limited by discrete padding steps.
*   **Time Complexity:** Proportional to the number of volume slices and the cost of 3D FFTs.
*   **Memory Complexity:** High, due to storing complex frequency domain data.
*   **When to use:** High-quality offline rendering of well-sampled (Nyquist-compliant) volume data where artifact-free zooming is critical.
*   **When not to use:** Real-time applications, or data with significant aliasing/noise without pre-filtering.
It builds on the Shear-Warp factorization [Lac95] and applies signal processing theorems (shifting, packing, derivative) to volume rendering.
It addresses the blurring artifacts of spatial domain interpolation by using the ideal sinc filter in the frequency domain.
